newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope, Anglican leader, urge mutual understanding.
newsitem.headline: Pope, Anglican leader, urge mutual understanding.

text.p: Pope John Paul and the leader of the world's Anglicans, Archbishop of Canterbury George Carey, urged each other on Thursday to understand their different positions in the difficult dialogue on Christian unity.

Both Church leaders reaffirmed their commitment to seeking greater unity in the approach to the year 2000, the start of Christianity's third millennium, in published speeches during a formal audience at the Vatican.

But without specifying the differences that separate their denominations, notably over women priests and the issue of papal primacy, the Pope and Carey spoke of difficulties and disappointments in the 30-year Roman Catholic-Anglican dialogue.

"Sadly these difficulties seem to loom large on the way to the reconciliation which the dialogue intended to promote," the 76-year-old Pope told Carey, who is spiritual leader of the 70- million-member worldwide Anglican Communion.

"My particular responsibility as the Successor of Peter for the faith and unity of the Church leads me to invite my brothers and sisters of the Anglican Communion to reflect on the motives and reasons of the positions I have expressed in the exercise of my teaching office," the Pope said.
Carey, who is on his first official visit to the Vatican, said obstacles had been "seen by some as obstruding themselves into the path of swift progress towards full, visible unity".
"However, as ecumenical partners we are called to affirm the integrity of the other, knowing that decisions will sometimes be made which we ourselves find difficult," Carey said.

Carey became Anglican leader in 1990. Two years later the Church of England, mother church of Anglicanism, voted to allow women priests in a move that severely tested relations between Canterbury and Rome. The first were ordained in 1994.
Recognition of the Pope's supreme authority over any unified Christian Church, or papal primacy, has been another thorny issue testing the Catholic-Anglican dialogue.
The Pope said in a 1995 encyclical that for the sake of unity he was willing to seek an accommodation with other Christian denominations on the future role of the papacy.

The Pope and Carey were due later on Thursday to worship together at the church of San Gregorio al Celio, from where St Augustine, the first archbishop of Canterbury, set out for England 1,400 years ago.
The Church of England was founded in the 1530s when King Henry VIII issued an act denying papal jurisdiction and broke with Rome.
Carey is due to visit Milan on Friday before returning to Britain.
